passage: On his first day in the new office tower, Deepak spent two minutes walking the corridor to find both stairwells, then went back to his desk. Mahima, at the next desk, raised an eyebrow. "Fire inspector?" "Habit," he said. In July the city's official alert turned orange for heavy rain by evening. Deepak read it, looked at the clear sky, and packed up at three. In his backpack sat the same small pouch as always: a torch, a water bottle, a charged power bank, a folded plastic sheet. "The sky looks fine," Mahima said. "Everyone else is staying." "Then I'll look silly tomorrow," he said, smiling. The rain came, but lighter than forecast. Next morning Mahima grinned. "Your big escape?" "Worth it," Deepak said, and meant it. "I'd rather be teased than stuck on the flyover till midnight."

qa.q: What was in Deepak's pouch?
qa.a: A torch, a water bottle, a charged power bank and a folded plastic sheet.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel about being teased the next morning?
qa.a: Relaxed and unbothered 🙂 He said "Worth it" and meant it, because a little teasing mattered far less to him than being stuck on the flyover.

qa.q: Why was leaving at three a sound choice even though the rain came lighter than forecast?
qa.a: Deepak followed the official alert rather than the clear sky, and the cost of being wrong was only some teasing, much smaller than being stranded.

qa.q: How might Mahima come to see Deepak's habits?
qa.a: At first Mahima finds them funny, but seeing Deepak calmly accept looking silly may make Mahima wonder whether staying late in a storm alert was the wiser choice.

grounding: A young man notes exits, carries a small kit, and leaves on an official rain alert, accepting teasing over the risk of being stuck.

passage: "Dilnaz, get your charger. We're going to Khala's tonight." "Because of one SMS?" Dilnaz didn't move from the sofa. "Zeenat Aapa, the road is dry." "The dam is releasing water after midnight. The message says low-lying areas. That's us." "You said the same last year and nothing happened." "And we lost nothing." Zeenat pulled the go-bag down from the top of the cupboard: medicines, torch, copies of the papers, two water bottles. "Kit's ready. It takes us fifteen minutes." "The neighbours will laugh." "Let them. If the water doesn't come, you can make fun of me all week. I'll even buy the samosas." Dilnaz groaned but reached for her shoes. "Double samosas." "Deal. Lock the balcony door."

qa.q: What was in the go-bag?
qa.a: Medicines, a torch, copies of the papers and two water bottles.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz worried about, apart from the water?
qa.a: That the neighbours would laugh at them for leaving because of one SMS 😅

qa.q: Which earlier choice made leaving easy for Zeenat?
qa.a: Keeping the go-bag packed in the cupboard, so following the warning took fifteen minutes instead of a long scramble.

qa.q: What would change if Zeenat waited until the road was wet before leaving?
qa.a: By then the water might already be rising around the house, and the calm trip to Khala's could become a rushed and risky one.

grounding: A young woman follows an official dam-release message without waiting for proof, with a ready kit and a joke about being wrong.

passage: I'm Suraj, and I've made peace with being the uncool friend. Last month Wasim and I went to a crowded music night in an old hall. Before sitting down, I did my usual thing and found the two exits, one beside the stage and one behind the snack counter. Wasim laughed. Halfway through, the lights flickered and a burning smell drifted in. A staff member took the mic: "As a precaution, please make your way outside." Plenty of people stayed put, filming the stage. I didn't wait to see smoke. I tapped Wasim, said "Let's go," and walked to the counter exit. He followed, grumbling. It turned out to be a burnt fuse in the kitchen. We missed three songs, and Wasim teased me all the way home. My face went warm, sure. But a warm face is a small price. I'd rather be early and wrong than late and right.

qa.q: What had caused the burning smell?
qa.a: A burnt fuse in the kitchen.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel while Wasim teased on the way home?
qa.a: A little embarrassed, with a warm face, but at peace with it, seeing it as a small price to pay.

qa.q: What habit made Suraj's quick exit possible?
qa.a: Finding the two exits before sitting down, so when the staff member asked people to go outside, Suraj knew exactly where to walk.

qa.q: How might Wasim see the evening, having followed Suraj out?
qa.a: Wasim missed three songs and enjoyed the teasing, but was also outside early and safe in case it had been serious.

grounding: A young adult checks exits in advance and follows a staff warning straight away, accepting mild embarrassment when it proves a false alarm.

passage:
Guest note, hill homestay near Madikeri. Yamini Poovaiah, owner.
Vaibhav, 25, checked in on Monday. Within ten minutes he had asked me where the cottage's second exit was and whether there was a torch by the bed. I noticed a small pouch clipped to his daypack: torch, whistle, water, copies of his ID.
On Wednesday afternoon the district issued a landslide advisory for our road and asked visitors to move to town. Most guests stayed on the veranda with their coffee; the rain didn't look like much. Vaibhav packed within twenty minutes. He said, "I'll feel silly if nothing happens, but that's better than being stuck." The others teased him a little.
Nothing happened on our road. On Friday he messaged to thank us and said he'd come back in the dry season.
Since then, I have pinned the district helpline numbers and exit map by every door.

qa.q: What was in the pouch clipped to Vaibhav's daypack?
qa.a: A torch, a whistle, water and copies of his ID.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav's remark about feeling silly show about his thinking?
qa.a: He expected possible embarrassment but judged it a small price compared with being stuck, so he acted on the advisory without waiting for proof.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav's habits make leaving early easy, and what did Yamini do next?
qa.a: Knowing the exits and keeping a small kit let him pack in twenty minutes; Yamini then pinned helpline numbers and exit maps by every door.

qa.q: How might the guests who teased Vaibhav think about it later?
qa.a: They might feel he overreacted since nothing happened, or quietly wonder what they would have done if the road had gone.

grounding: An adult notes exits, carries a small kit and leaves on an official warning, accepting the risk of a false alarm.

passage:
12 March, Port Blair

The ground swayed around eleven, a long slow roll. Twenty minutes later the official alert came: possible tsunami, move away from the shore to higher ground. Francis, across from me at the seafront café, laughed and ordered another tea. "These come every few months, yaar. Never anything."
I already had my small bag: water, torch, charger, ID copies. Last month I'd walked the route up the hill to the church, so I knew it took twelve minutes. I paid and went. I felt very dramatic walking past everyone still eating.
The alert was withdrawn at two. Nothing came. Francis sent a photo of his third tea: "Survived, hero 🙂"
Yes, I felt stupid for about ten minutes. But stupid is fine. Late isn't. Same thing next time.
Samir

qa.q: How long did Samir's walk up the hill to the church take?
qa.a: It took twelve minutes.

qa.q: How did Samir feel walking past everyone still eating?
qa.a: Samir felt dramatic and a little foolish, but was still more concerned about being late than about looking silly.

qa.q: What did Samir's preparation do well?
qa.a: Having a small bag ready and having walked the route before meant Samir could follow the alert at once, without debating it.

qa.q: How might Francis see Samir's leaving, and what would change if the wave had come?
qa.a: Francis sees it as funny overcaution; if the wave had come, Francis would have been the one caught at the shore while Samir was already safe.

grounding: An adult follows an official tsunami alert at once with a ready kit and known route, preferring embarrassment to being late.

passage:
The panchayat loudspeaker crackled just after lunch: the river upstream was rising, families near the ghat should move to the high school by evening.
Shreya had been teaching in the village for a year. She lived in two rooms near the ghat. The cloth bag she kept by the door already held a torch, a water bottle, her ID papers and a few biscuits. She picked it up, locked the school cupboard with the registers inside, and walked up the slope.
Tanvir, who ran the tea stall, laughed. "Madam, the river always talks and never comes."
"Then I'll have tea at the high school instead," she said, cheeks warm.
She sat on the steps there with three old women and a goat. By night the river had risen to the ghat's third step and stopped.
Tanvir brought her tea next morning. "So, madam. Nothing." She laughed with him.

qa.q: What was in Shreya's cloth bag?
qa.a: A torch, a water bottle, her ID papers and a few biscuits.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel when Tanvir laughed at her?
qa.a: She felt a little embarrassed, with warm cheeks, but calm and settled in her choice to go early.

qa.q: What does Shreya's approach do well?
qa.a: Keeping a ready bag and acting on the announcement straight away meant she was safe without panic or delay, and she could laugh at the false alarm afterwards.

qa.q: Why might Tanvir react so differently to the loudspeaker?
qa.a: He has seen the river rise without flooding many times, so the warning feels ordinary to him and moving seems like an overreaction.

grounding: It shows an adult acting on an official flood warning with a ready kit and accepting mild embarrassment when it did not flood.

passage:
Aiko always found the exits first. On her first night in the new flat in Sendai, before she unpacked, she walked the corridor to the stairwell and counted doors. Her small backpack with water, a torch and spare socks sat by the shoe rack.
Two weeks later her phone blared an earthquake alert while she and Mei were eating noodles. The floor rolled gently for a few seconds. Then a tsunami advisory came up for the coast.
"We're three kilometres inland," Mei said, still holding her chopsticks.
"The advisory says go up," Aiko said, already putting on her shoes.
They climbed to the school on the hill with the backpack and sat among families in blankets. Around midnight the advisory was lifted; the sea had risen only a little.
"All that for nothing," Mei said.
"I'd rather be a bit silly on a hill," Aiko said, a little red, and shared the torch.

qa.q: What was in Aiko's small backpack?
qa.a: Water, a torch and spare socks.

qa.q: What was Aiko feeling when she said she would rather be a bit silly on a hill?
qa.a: She felt a little embarrassed, but settled and sure that acting early was the right choice.

qa.q: What could Mei take from Aiko's approach?
qa.a: Following official advisories straight away and keeping a small kit ready means you are not deciding in a hurry when something happens.

qa.q: How might Mei see the night on the hill?
qa.a: She seems to think it was a waste at first, though she still went along, and she may see more sense in it next time.

grounding: It shows an adult who notes exits, keeps a small kit and follows an official advisory without waiting for proof, accepting a false alarm.

passage:
At the three-day training at the convention centre in Pune, Omkar did what he always did on the first morning: he walked the corridor and counted doors to the nearest exit. Four doors, then the green sign. His colleague Vaibhav laughed. "Planning an escape from the lecture?"
On day two, halfway through a session, the alarm sounded. The speaker paused. People looked at each other. Omkar picked up his bag, which held his phone, a torch and a small first-aid pouch, and walked out, counting doors. A few people followed.
On the lawn, the organisers announced a faulty sensor. Vaibhav grinned. "All that for nothing." Omkar shrugged. "I'd rather be embarrassed on a lawn than late on the stairs."

qa.q: What was in Omkar's bag?
qa.a: His phone, a torch and a small first-aid pouch.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when Vaibhav teased him on the lawn?
qa.a: Omkar seemed calm and unbothered, preferring a little embarrassment to being late in a real emergency.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's habits would help in a real fire?
qa.a: Knowing the exit route in advance and leaving at once with a small kit, without waiting for proof.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see these habits after a real emergency?
qa.a: He might feel grateful and see them as sensible rather than funny.

grounding: Shows an adult who notes exits, carries a small kit and leaves at the first alarm, accepting the mild embarrassment of a false alarm.

passage:
Dear Hemant,
Since you've just moved to Vizag, here's what I learned in my first cyclone season. When the official warning came in October, most of my neighbours said, "Let's see if it actually hits." I didn't wait. I already had a small kit by the door: torch, power bank, water, dry snacks, copies of documents in a zip bag, my medicines. I had checked the route to the community hall.
When the district told our street to move, I went that afternoon. The cyclone turned north; our street got only rain. Some people teased me for running away. I felt a bit silly, honestly. But silly and safe is a good trade.
Please make your kit this weekend.
Love, Lavanya

qa.q: In which month did the official warning come?
qa.a: In October.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel about being teased by the neighbours?
qa.a: Lavanya felt a bit silly but still sure that being safe was worth it.

qa.q: What should Hemant do this weekend?
qa.a: Make a small kit like Lavanya's and learn the routes to safe places near the new home.

qa.q: How might the neighbours who waited have felt when the cyclone turned?
qa.a: They may have felt relieved and confident, perhaps not noticing how lucky they had been.

grounding: A young adult's letter describes keeping a small kit, knowing routes and following an official warning early, preferring embarrassment to being late.

passage:
Divyansh, you asked about my gas leak story for the podcast. Sure. I'm Ankita, and I'm the person who leaves first. One night last winter I smelled gas in our building corridor. Faint, but there. My neighbours said, "It's always a bit smelly, it's the old pipes." I didn't argue.
I opened the windows, didn't touch any switches, knocked on two doors, went downstairs and called the gas company's emergency line, like the sticker by the meter says. Then I waited outside in my pyjamas for forty minutes. They found a small loose joint and fixed it. Nothing dramatic.
Everyone came down to see why I was out in the cold in pyjamas. I was embarrassed. But I'd do it again tomorrow.

qa.q: How long did Ankita wait outside?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel standing outside in pyjamas?
qa.a: Ankita felt embarrassed in front of the neighbours, yet sure the choice was right.

qa.q: Which of Ankita's steps followed the official advice?
qa.a: Calling the gas company's emergency line, as the sticker by the meter says, after opening windows and avoiding switches.

qa.q: How might the neighbours see Ankita now?
qa.a: They might see Ankita as over-careful, or feel grateful once they learn about the loose joint.

grounding: A young adult describes acting on a faint gas smell at once and following the official instructions, preferring mild embarrassment to waiting for proof.

passage:
Ankita moved into the flat next to ours in Kochi last year, and I've watched her do things I thought were a bit much. The first week, she walked the building's stairwells and noted both exits on a sticky note by her door. She keeps a small bag by the shoe rack: torch, water bottles, copies of her documents, a charger. In August, when the district sent a heavy-rain alert, she moved her scooter to higher ground and left for her sister's place that same evening. The rest of us laughed. The water only came up to the gate, and she came back two days later. I asked if she felt silly. She shrugged and said, 'A bit. I'd rather be a bit silly than late.' I don't know what she was really feeling. But last week I bought a torch.

Aadhya

qa.a: A torch, water bottles, copies of her documents and a charger.

qa.q: How did Ankita seem to feel about leaving early when the water stayed at the gate?
qa.a: Ankita seemed a little embarrassed but calm and unbothered, preferring feeling silly to being late.

qa.q: Which of Ankita's habits could anyone copy?
qa.a: Noting exits, keeping a small emergency bag, and acting on official warnings without waiting for proof.

qa.q: How has Aadhya been affected by watching Ankita?
qa.a: Aadhya went from laughing at her to buying a torch, quietly starting to prepare too.

grounding: An observer describes an adult who notes exits, keeps a kit and follows warnings early, accepting the mild embarrassment of a false alarm.

passage:
Week one. Tejas moved into his first flat in Mumbai and, before unpacking, walked the stairs to find both exits. His cousin Eshaan, helping with boxes, laughed. 'Planning an escape?'

Week three. Tejas packed a small bag: torch, water, a phone charger, copies of his ID. He put it by the door. Eshaan rolled his eyes but said nothing.

Week seven. The city issued an orange alert for heavy rain at 5 pm. Tejas left the office at once and was home before the trains stopped. Eshaan, who had stayed to finish a report, spent the night on a platform. The next morning he texted Tejas: 'Okay. Exits and bag. Show me how.'

qa.q: What did Tejas put by the door in week three?
qa.a: A small bag with a torch, water, a phone charger and copies of his ID.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when Eshaan laughed at him in week one?
qa.a: Tejas may have felt a little embarrassed, but calm and sure it was worth doing.

qa.q: What choice in week seven made the difference?
qa.a: Leaving the office as soon as the alert came, without waiting for proof that the trains would stop.

qa.q: How does Eshaan's view change over the weeks?
qa.a: Eshaan goes from mocking to asking Tejas to show him how, after a night on the platform.

grounding: An adult notes exits, keeps a small kit and follows official warnings early, accepting mild embarrassment over being late.

passage: Gurpreet puttar, you laugh at my torch and water by the door? Sit, let your Siddharth Taya tell you why. In 1998 I was a young man of twenty-five, working in the mill office in Ludhiana. There was an earthquake warning on the radio. Most people shrugged. I went home early and moved my parents out of the old brick room into the courtyard for the night. The neighbours laughed; my friend Harpal called me 'Earthquake Singh' for months. Nothing happened that night. I felt foolish, I won't lie. But two years later, when the floods came, I was the one who left early, and I had a bag ready. Harpal's family lost their papers. So yes, puttar, I'll take a little laughing over being late.

qa.q: In which year did the earthquake warning come?
How did Siddharth feel when nothing happened that night?
qa.a: Siddharth felt foolish and embarrassed, especially with Harpal's teasing.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Leaving early with a ready bag when the floods came, because acting on warnings kept his family's papers safe while Harpal's were lost.

qa.q: How might Harpal's family have felt after the floods?
qa.a: Harpal's family probably felt shaken and regretful, having lost their papers by not acting early.

grounding: An elder explains why he follows warnings early and keeps a kit, preferring the embarrassment of a false alarm to being late.

passage:
The official alert buzzed at 10:40 p.m.: heavy rain, low-lying streets may flood, move to higher floors. Zeenat's phone was on eleven percent and the power had just gone. Her flatmate Jyoti was stuck at her office across the city.
Zeenat didn't wait to see water at the door. She pulled out the small bag she kept under her bed: torch, copies of her papers, a charger, biscuits, a water bottle. She texted Jyoti, "Going up to Mrs. Pillai on the third floor. Your laptop is with me." She had walked the back staircase the week she moved in, so she climbed it in the dark without fumbling.
The landlord chuckled on the landing. "Madam, this street never floods."
By morning the water had only reached the gate. Zeenat felt a bit silly carrying her bag back down, but she was smiling.

qa.q: What was in the bag Zeenat kept under the bed?
qa.a: A torch, copies of her papers, a charger, biscuits and a water bottle.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel carrying the bag back down in the morning?
qa.a: She felt a bit silly, but she was smiling, content that a small embarrassment was better than being caught by rising water.

qa.q: Which of Zeenat's habits helped most when the alert came late at night?
qa.a: Keeping a packed bag and knowing the back staircase let her act in the dark, on a low phone, without waiting for proof.

qa.q: What was it like for Jyoti, stuck across the city, to get Zeenat's text?
qa.a: Jyoti probably felt relieved to know where Zeenat was and that the laptop was safe, instead of worrying all night.

grounding: An adult follows an official flood alert at night with a ready bag and a known exit, accepting the mild embarrassment of a false alarm.
